introduction-why-dockerize-everything-fa.core: Mobile and desktop builds depend on proprietary toolchains (Xcode only runs on macOS, signing tied to Apple and Google accounts) and real hardware, so Linux containers can't solve them. CI needs special runners, signing automation and device testing.

first_principles.problem: A backend team's container-only CI can't build iOS apps at all.
truths: Xcode requires macOS on Apple hardware.
derivation: Provision **macOS runners**.
Automate **code signing**.
Script releases with **Fastlane**.
Test on **device farms**.

analogy.title: Walled gardens
analogy.story: Each app store is a gated garden with its own rules, tools and gatekeepers.
analogy.breaks: Android builds can run on Linux containers; iOS and macOS can't.

example.title: One app, two platforms

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each platform gets the infrastructure it requires.

example.outcome: mobile CI built around its real constraints.

check.q: Why can't iOS apps be built in standard Linux containers?
check.a: Xcode only runs on macOS, which Apple's licence restricts to Apple hardware.

the-specific-hell-of-mac-runners.core: Apple's EULA restricts macOS to Apple hardware, so Mac CI capacity is scarce and expensive: hosted macOS minutes cost far more, cloud Mac instances have 24-hour minimum allocations, and self-hosted Mac minis need fleet management.

first_principles.problem: iOS builds queue for hours on a few Mac machines, while Linux jobs start instantly.
truths: Licensing ties macOS to Apple hardware.
Mac capacity can't burst like Linux.
derivation: **Hosted** macOS runners: easy but costly.
**Cloud Macs** (EC2 mac, 24h minimum allocation) or **Mac fleets** (MacStadium, self-hosted minis).
**Virtualise** with Tart/Anka for clean ephemeral VMs.
Minimise Mac minutes: run **Linux for everything else**.

analogy.title: A rare specialist doctor
analogy.story: Only a few can perform the procedure, so you book carefully and handle prep elsewhere.
analogy.breaks: Apple Silicon versus Intel differences add yet another dimension.

example.title: Cutting Mac minutes
flow: Linux: lint, Swift unit tests (Linux-compatible parts)
Mac: only xcodebuild archive + UI tests

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Mac usage halved and the queue shortened.

example.outcome: Mac capacity is used where it's truly needed.

check.q: Why do cloud Mac instances often have a 24-hour minimum?
check.a: Apple's licensing requires dedicated hardware allocations with a minimum lease period.

code-signing-the-identity-crisis.core: Every iOS binary must be signed with a certificate and a provisioning profile that matches the app ID, devices and entitlements. CI needs those secrets available securely and reproducibly, without the keychain chaos of personal Macs.

first_principles.problem: Builds fail with 'no matching provisioning profile' because certificates live on one developer's laptop.
truths: Apple ties signing identities to team accounts.
Profiles expire and must match exactly.
derivation: Store certificates and profiles **encrypted** in a repo or cloud bucket (fastlane match).
Create a **temporary keychain** per CI job.
Use **App Store Connect API keys**, not personal Apple IDs.
**Rotate** and audit.

analogy.title: A notarised identity document
analogy.story: Without the official stamp matching your name and destination, the border won't let the package through.
analogy.breaks: Android signing is simpler (a keystore), but losing the upload key is still painful.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Any runner can sign, and nothing lives on personal machines.

code.text:
lane :beta do
  setup_ci                       # temp keychain
  match(type: "appstore", readonly: true)
  build_app(scheme: "App")
end

check.a: Encrypted, shared iOS certificates and provisioning profiles for the team and CI.

fastlane-the-automation-savior.core: Fastlane wraps the painful mobile release steps (building, signing, screenshots, metadata, TestFlight and Play Store uploads) into Ruby 'lanes' that run the same way locally and in CI.

first_principles.problem: Releasing an app means 30 manual clicks across Xcode, App Store Connect and the Play Console.
truths: Store APIs exist but are complex.
derivation: Define **lanes** in a Fastfile (test, beta, release).
Use **actions**: build_app, match, upload_to_testflight, supply.
Run lanes **in CI** with API keys.
Version **metadata** in Git.

analogy.title: A universal remote for app stores
analogy.story: One button sequence does what used to need many devices and menus.
analogy.breaks: Fastlane depends on Ruby, and Apple API changes can break actions temporarily.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: `fastlane beta` ships to testers in one command.

code.text:
lane :beta do
  increment_build_number(build_number: ENV["GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER"])
  match(type: "appstore", readonly: true)
  build_app(scheme: "App")
  upload_to_testflight(api_key_path: "asc_key.json")
end

check.q: What Fastlane action uploads Android builds to Google Play?

device-farms-real-hardware-testing.core: Simulators and emulators miss real-device issues: memory pressure, GPU and camera behaviour, OEM Android quirks, network conditions. Device farms (Firebase Test Lab, AWS Device Farm, BrowserStack) run tests on real phones in CI.

first_principles.problem: The app passes every simulator test but crashes on a 3-year-old Samsung with low memory.
truths: Device fragmentation is huge on Android.
Buying every device yourself is impractical.
derivation: Run **unit and simulator tests** on every PR (fast).
Run a **device farm** matrix nightly or before release.
Choose devices by **user analytics** (top models and OS versions).
Collect **videos, logs and performance** data.

analogy.title: Crash-testing real cars, not just simulations
analogy.story: Simulations are cheap, but you still crash a real car before selling it.
analogy.breaks: Device farms are slower and cost per minute, so be selective.

example.title: A pre-release device matrix

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: An OOM crash on the A51 is fixed before release.

code.text:
gcloud firebase test android run --app app.apk --test app-test.apk \
  --device model=a51,version=31 --device model=oriole,version=34

example.outcome: releases are validated on the devices users actually own.

check.q: Why use device farms in addition to simulators?
check.a: Real devices reveal hardware, memory, OEM and performance issues that simulators miss.
